regions.Superior Frontal: Upper part of the frontal lobe. Involved in self-awareness, working memory and planning; its medial part includes the supplementary motor area, which prepares movements.
regions.Rostral Middle Frontal: Front part of the middle frontal gyrus, part of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex: working memory, planning and cognitive control.
regions.Caudal Middle Frontal: Back part of the middle frontal gyrus, including the frontal eye fields that steer voluntary eye movements and attention.
regions.Pars Opercularis: Back part of the inferior frontal gyrus. On the left it forms part of Broca's area, important for speech production and grammar.
regions.Pars Triangularis: Middle part of the inferior frontal gyrus. On the left it is part of Broca's area, involved in language and word meaning.
regions.Pars Orbitalis: Front, lowest part of the inferior frontal gyrus, involved in language meaning and in linking reward with behaviour.
regions.Lateral Orbitofrontal: Underside of the frontal lobe, above the eyes. Evaluates rewards and punishments and helps adjust behaviour when outcomes change.
regions.Medial Orbitofrontal: Underside of the frontal lobe near the midline. Represents value and is involved in decision-making and emotion.
regions.Precentral: Primary motor cortex. Each part controls movement of one body part, laid out as a map of the body (the motor homunculus).
regions.Paracentral: Where motor and sensory cortex continue onto the inner (medial) surface; controls and senses the legs and feet.
regions.Postcentral: Primary somatosensory cortex: touch, pressure, temperature and body position, mapped body part by body part.
regions.Superior Parietal: Upper parietal lobe. Combines vision and body position to guide reaching and to direct spatial attention.
regions.Inferior Parietal: Lower parietal lobe, including the angular gyrus. Involved in attention, reading, arithmetic and understanding others' actions.
regions.Supramarginal: Part of the inferior parietal lobe. Involved in phonological (sound-based) language processing, touch perception and tool use.
regions.Precuneus: Medial parietal cortex. Involved in visual imagery, memory recall and self-related thought; a core hub of the default mode network.
regions.Superior Temporal: Upper temporal gyrus. Processes sounds and speech; on the left its back part includes Wernicke's area for language comprehension.
regions.Transverse Temporal: Heschl's gyrus, the primary auditory cortex, where sound first reaches the cortex.
regions.Middle Temporal: Middle temporal gyrus. Involved in word meaning and semantic memory; its back part is close to motion-sensitive area MT.
regions.Inferior temporal: Lower temporal gyrus, the end of the ventral visual stream ('IT'): recognises objects and faces.
regions.Fusiform: Underside of the temporal and occipital lobes. Contains areas specialised for faces (fusiform face area) and written words.
regions.Parahippocampal: Next to the hippocampus. Processes scenes and places and supports memory formation.
regions.Entorhinal: Gateway between the cortex and the hippocampus; contains grid cells that support navigation and memory.
regions.Lateral Occipital: Outer occipital cortex. Processes shapes and objects (the lateral occipital complex).
regions.Cuneus: Medial occipital lobe above the calcarine sulcus; early visual processing of the lower visual field.
regions.Lingual: Medial occipital lobe below the calcarine sulcus; early visual processing of the upper visual field, colour and letters.
regions.Pericalcarine: Around the calcarine sulcus: primary visual cortex (V1), where visual information first reaches the cortex.
regions.Rostral Anterior Cingulate: Front of the cingulate cortex. Involved in emotion regulation and mood.
regions.Caudal Anterior Cingulate: Monitors conflict and errors and helps adjust behaviour; a source of frontal midline theta and the error-related negativity in EEG.
regions.Posterior Cingulate: Part of the default mode network; active during mind-wandering, autobiographical memory and self-related thought.
regions.Isthmus Cingulate: Narrow back part of the cingulate cortex, linking it to the parahippocampal region; involved in memory and spatial orientation.
regions.Insula: Hidden deep in the lateral sulcus. Senses the body's internal state (heartbeat, breathing), and is involved in taste, pain and emotion.
regions.Thalamus: Central relay station: almost all sensory information passes through it on the way to the cortex. Thalamo-cortical loops help generate EEG rhythms such as alpha and sleep spindles.
regions.Caudate: Part of the basal ganglia (striatum). Involved in learning, goal-directed behaviour and movement control.
regions.Putamen: Part of the basal ganglia (striatum). Involved in movement and habit learning; affected early in Parkinson's disease.
regions.Pallidum: Globus pallidus, an output station of the basal ganglia that regulates movement.
regions.Hippocampus: Essential for forming new memories and for spatial navigation.
regions.Amygdala: Detects emotionally important events, especially threats, and supports emotional learning.
regions.Accumbens Area: Nucleus accumbens, part of the reward system; involved in motivation and pleasure.
regions.Ventral Diencephalon: Region including the hypothalamus and nearby structures; regulates hormones, body temperature, hunger and sleep.
regions.Basal Forebrain: Contains cholinergic neurons that project widely to the cortex and support attention and memory.
regions.Brainstem: Connects the brain with the spinal cord and controls vital functions such as breathing and heart rate; also regulates arousal and sleep.
regions.Optic Chiasm: Where the optic nerves cross, so each hemisphere receives information about the opposite half of the visual field.
regions.Cerebellum Gray Matter: The cerebellum's cortex: coordinates movement, balance and timing, and also contributes to some cognitive functions.
regions.Cerebellum White Matter: Fibre pathways carrying information into and out of the cerebellar cortex.
regions.Vermal lobules I-V: Front part of the cerebellar vermis (midline); involved in posture and balance.
regions.Vermal lobules VI-VII: Middle part of the vermis; involved in eye movements and coordination.
regions.Vermal lobules VIII-X: Back part of the vermis; involved in balance and eye movements.
regions.Lateral Ventricle: Fluid-filled space (cerebrospinal fluid) inside each hemisphere. Not neural tissue.
regions.Inferior Lateral Ventricle: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, a fluid-filled space next to the hippocampus.
regions.Third Ventricle: Fluid-filled space between the two halves of the thalamus.
regions.Fourth Ventricle: Fluid-filled space between the brainstem and the cerebellum.

electrodes.Fp1: Frontal pole, left. Very sensitive to eye blinks and eye movements, so it is often used to detect and remove these artifacts.
electrodes.Fpz: Frontal pole, midline. Often used as the ground electrode, and very sensitive to eye blinks.
electrodes.Fp2: Frontal pole, right. Very sensitive to eye blinks and eye movements, often used to detect these artifacts.
electrodes.F7: Left inferior frontal region, over Broca's area. Picks up horizontal eye movements; relevant for language-related activity.
electrodes.F3: Left dorsolateral frontal cortex. Used in studies of working memory and of frontal alpha asymmetry (linked to motivation and mood).
electrodes.Fz: Frontal midline. Frontal midline theta (4–7 Hz) increases with concentration and working memory; also records the P3a and error-related responses.
electrodes.F4: Right dorsolateral frontal cortex. Paired with F3 in frontal alpha asymmetry studies.
electrodes.F8: Right inferior frontal region. Picks up horizontal eye movements; the right inferior frontal cortex is involved in stopping actions.
electrodes.T7: Left temporal (old name T3), over auditory and language cortex. Often affected by jaw and temporal muscle artifacts; clinically important in temporal lobe epilepsy.
electrodes.C3: Over the left motor and sensory hand area. Records the mu rhythm (8–13 Hz), which drops when the right hand moves or when movement is imagined: the basis of many motor-imagery BCIs.
electrodes.Cz: Vertex (top of the head). Over the leg and foot motor areas; auditory N1/P2 responses are strongest here. Often used as a reference electrode.
electrodes.C4: Over the right motor and sensory hand area. Its mu rhythm drops with left-hand movement or imagery; paired with C3 in motor-imagery BCIs.
electrodes.T8: Right temporal (old name T4), over auditory cortex. Often affected by muscle artifacts.
electrodes.P7: Left temporo-parietal-occipital (old name T5). Near visual areas for objects and written words; records the N170 to faces and words.
electrodes.P3: Left parietal. Involved in spatial attention and number processing; posterior alpha changes with attention.
electrodes.Pz: Parietal midline. The P300 (P3b) response, used in oddball experiments and P300 spellers, is usually largest here.
electrodes.P4: Right parietal. Involved in spatial attention; paired with P3 in attention studies.
electrodes.P8: Right temporo-parietal-occipital (old name T6). The face-sensitive N170 is often largest around here.
electrodes.O1: Left occipital, over visual cortex. Alpha rhythm (8–13 Hz) is strongest here with the eyes closed; records visual evoked potentials.
electrodes.Oz: Occipital midline, over primary visual cortex. Records the P100 visual evoked potential and steady-state visual responses (SSVEP).
electrodes.O2: Right occipital, over visual cortex. Alpha rhythm is strongest here with the eyes closed; records visual evoked potentials.
